title: Tributary glacier surges: an exceptional concentration at Panmah Glacier, Karakoram Himalaya
abstract: Abstract Four tributaries of Panmah Glacier have surged in less than a decade, three in quick succession between 2001 and 2005. Since 1985, 13 surges have been recorded in the Karakoram Himalaya, more than in any comparable period since the 1850s. Ten were tributary surges. In these ten a full run-out of surge ice is prevented, but extended post-surge episodes affect the tributary and main glacier. The sudden concentration of events at Panmah Glacier is without precedent and at odds with known surge intervals for the glaciers. Interpretations must consider the response of thermally complex glaciers, at exceptionally high altitudes and of high relief, to changes in a distinctive regional climate. It is suggested that high-altitude warming affecting snow and glacier thermal regimes, or bringing intense, short-term melting episodes, may be more significant than mass-balance change.
problem: The paper addresses the challenge of explaining the unprecedented, sudden concentration of tributary glacier surges in the Karakoram, as these clustered events are at odds with known surge intervals and cannot be explained by simple mass-balance changes alone, suggesting alternative high-altitude climatic drivers are more significant.
method: The paper proposes that the exceptional concentration of glacier surges is a response to high-altitude warming affecting glacier thermal regimes and causing intense, short-term melting episodes, which may be a more significant driver than gradual mass-balance change.
task: The task is to interpret the exceptional concentration of recent tributary glacier surges at Panmah Glacier, proposing that high-altitude warming affecting snow and thermal regimes is a more significant driver than mass-balance change.
innovation: This paper documents an unprecedented concentration of tributary glacier surges at Panmah Glacier, proposing that high-altitude warming affecting glacier thermal regimes, rather than mass-balance change, is the more significant trigger for this recent cluster of events.

The 1995 Chiring Glacier surge was described by Hewitt (1998). By the summer of 2005, marked thickening was observed in its accumulation zone. The entire ablation zone had thinned to 10-50 m below the 1996 profile. It was no longer heavily crevassed but remained active throughout. Tributaries sheared off in the surge have now adjusted to enter at the present ice level.

Maedan Glacier surged some time after 2002, causing major thickening and break-up of its lower 8 km (Fig. 2). Along the side-walls were masses of dirty ice, in places more than 100 m above pre- and post-surge levels, evidence of a 'mid-glacier zone' of the surge, with 'compressive followed by extensive flow' (Murray and others, 1998, p. 271). When observed in July 2005, the surge was over but the lower Maedan Glacier surface remained a mass of seracs. A smoother lobe of its ice, ~3 km² in area, had entered the main Nobande Sobande Glacier and formed a series of concentric ridges, with the highest at the outer rim, reflecting a zone of compression continuing after the surge. Opposite the junction, Chiring Glacier was compressed to a narrow, heavily crevassed thread. The lobe of the 1995 Chiring Glacier surge ice in the main valley was distorted by Maedan Glacier, but its outer rim was still a well-defined, steep-sided ridge of ice ~40–60 m high.

The Drenmang Glacier surge probably began in the fall or winter 2004/05, coming from the east branch, the larger of Drenmang Glacier's two main sources. When visited in 1996, and on Landsat imagery to 2001, ice from the shorter western branch occupied more than half the combined area beyond their junction. By the summer of 2005 this relationship was reversed. There were steep ice cliffs along both flanks of the eastern branch, and broken masses of dirty ice were overriding lateral moraines that had been ice-free for some decades (Fig. 5). The central areas were more crevassed than in 1996, but not as severely broken as on Shingchukpi or Maedan Glacier, perhaps because the surge was in an early stage.
